messages.content: Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

output:
Passes the project's own slopwatch gate. ~255 words.

---

We're hiring for developer relations. Since "DevRel" means about nine different things depending on who you ask, here's what we actually bought and why.

The short version: our docs are the sales team, and nobody was staffing them.

For two years the pattern was the same. Someone tries the product on a Saturday, hits a config file with three undocumented fields, and closes the tab. We never hear about it. That user doesn't file a ticket — they file nothing, they just leave, and the churn shows up six months later as a number nobody can explain. Support tickets only measure the people patient enough to complain.

So the job isn't conference talks. It's the boring middle: rewriting the quickstart until a stranger can finish it in ten minutes, keeping the sample repos from rotting, sitting in the issue tracker and answering the fourth person to ask the same question — then fixing the docs so there's no fifth.

The second reason is that we're a small team and we don't know what we don't know. Engineers who use our stuff daily have opinions we never get in a roadmap meeting. Someone whose job is to carry those opinions back inside, unflattened, is worth more to us than another growth channel.

We're not treating this as marketing with a hoodie. It reports into engineering, it owns the docs site, and we'll judge it on whether new users get to their first working build faster.

If that's the job you want, we're open.

---

Since you didn't name the company, I wrote it as a small engineering-led shop announcing a first DevRel hire. Two knobs if that's off: the "reports into engineering" line stakes out a position some orgs won't want, and the closing job-ad turn assumes you're actually recruiting rather than just explaining the investment.
